*   The text states that a CT venography was performed and it confirmed the DVT.

Since CT venography is a procedure (imaging procedure) and it explicitly confirmed the DVT, this option fits the evidence. The evidence explicitly states that a CT venography (a procedure) was performed and it confirmed the presence of DVT. is marked variability in the methodology used, making it difﬁcult
to have a reference standard. In patients older than 50 years, an
age-adjusted threshold should be used as normal D-dimer levels
increase with age [79]. Troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide
(BNP) are biomarkers of cardiac injury and can be used to assess

5.2.1. Clinical presentation
The Working Group agreed that DVT, and PE represent typical
venous events, and that stroke and myocardial infarction represent
typical arterial events. While rarer than DVT and PE, there are sev-
eral other recognized venous thrombosis syndromes involving
abdominal veins, cerebral veins, cerebral venous sinuses and reti-
nal veins. As an AESI, thrombosis and thromboembolism may be

The evidence describes a patient with symptoms in the right arm (redness, warmth, pain) associated with a central venous catheter. The diagnostic workup included a CT venography which confirmed "trombosi della vena succlavia destra" (right subclavian vein thrombosis). According to the Brighton criteria and general medical classification, upper extremity deep vein thrombosis is a form of DVT/VTE. The text does not mention any other disease process (such as cellulitis, muscle tear, or hematoma) that was identified as the cause of the illness. While cellulitis is listed as a possible alternative etiology in the reference material, the record explicitly confirms thrombosis via imaging and does not diagnose an alternative condition. Therefore, no alternative diagnosis explaining the acute illness was found; the confirmed diagnosis is DVT itself.
